problem: DRL for social navigation is mostly trained in simulators whose human models (e.g. ORCA) mismatch real human motion, and training directly in the real world is impractical because DRL needs lots of data and behaves unsafely at initialization.
motivation: The most accurate data for social navigation is real-world data, so agents should be trained directly on it without a sim-to-real gap. That requires a sample-efficient, safe-at-start learner. Classical path-tracking MPC is already optimal when no humans are present, so DRL should not have to relearn it.
key_idea: Blend MPC path tracking with model-free DRL by learning a state-dependent convex weight alpha between the MPC action and one of six candidate human-avoidance actions, initialized to near-MPC behaviour and guided by OOD detection plus a heuristic safety policy.
insight: Initializing with beta=-0.8 suppresses alpha so early behaviour is almost pure MPC, whereas plain residual DRL follows MPC only in expectation. In simulation, both DR-MPC variants reach SR 0.57/0.58 against 0.20 (naive DRL) and 0.21 (residual DRL). OOD detection with the heuristic policy mainly helps early training and converges to similar final performance. The reward ablation shows every reward term matters; removing r_hum-col drops SR to 0.24.
method: MDP formulation: human avoidance plus path tracking within constant-width virtual corridors; state = local path nodes (S_PT) + robot and human past positions (S_HA); action = (v, w); reward = path advancement, deviation, goal, corridor collision, min actuation, human collision, disturbance penalty.

Human Avoidance Network (HAN): a GRU per human trajectory, human-human multi-head attention, then robot-human attention. It is adapted from Intention-Aware Graph to use past rather than forecasted trajectories and to handle variable lengths. Outputs a crowd embedding.
Six candidate human-avoidance actions: the action space is split into 2 linear x 3 angular velocity cells, and each cell has a Gaussian-sampled action a_HA^i (TD3-style decaying variance).

Residual fusion: an MLP fuses the path embedding, crowd embedding, a_MPC and a_HA to produce alpha_i (SAC-style mean/log-std, tanh, plus a learned bias beta initialized at -0.8, clipped to [0,1]) and a categorical p over the six cells. The final action is a = alpha_j a_HA^j + (1-alpha_j) a_MPC with j~p.
Training: Discrete SAC with double average clipped Q-learning and Q-clip, plus the SAC entropy term for alpha; soft resets return the robot to the closest non-terminal state instead of hard resets.

OOD guidance: KNN (Faiss) in the model's latent space over the replay buffer, with a threshold equal to the mean distance between (S,S') pairs. For OOD states, a constant-velocity (CVMM) 2 s rollout checks safety; if unsafe, the heuristic policy picks the safe action closest to a_MPC. The KNN threshold is scaled by 1/3 early in training and relaxed to 1.

Real-world stack: Jackal with Ouster OS0-128 LiDAR; YOLOX on the reflectivity image plus depth for 3D human positions, Norfair tracking, LiDAR Teach-and-Repeat for localization and path, MPC path tracker (Sehn et al.).

setting.backbone: DR-MPC: GRU + multi-head attention HAN + MLPs, trained with Discrete SAC from scratch; MPC path tracker; YOLOX (pretrained) for detection
setting.training_data: Simulation: 37,500 steps (~2.5 h) in a CrowdNav-based simulator with 6 ORCA humans. Real world: 3.75 h (<4 h) of online experience, ~15 h wall-clock, no simulation.
setting.observation: single 360° LiDAR (range point cloud + reflectivity image), tracked human positions, robot velocity/position history, local path nodes
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (v, w), 0.2 s timestep real / 0.25 s sim
setting.simulator: Modified CrowdNav (2D, ORCA humans, path tracking in corridors); real-world Jackal
setting.privileged: none (in simulation, corridor and path are given; the real robot uses a taught path from T&R)

numbers.extra: 37,500 training steps (~2.5 h); averaged over 10 trials; 6 ORCA humans
3.75 h real-world training; 0-4 humans; the heuristic, Sim Model Raw and Sim Model Adjusted baselines are not included
numbers.evidence: Table 3 Real-world Policy Results (mean per loop), DR-MPC (Ours)

numbers_note: Not an R2R/ObjectNav-style benchmark; only custom simulation and real-world tests.
results: In simulation, DR-MPC reaches SR 0.57-0.58 against 0.20 for naive DRL and 0.21 for residual DRL, close to ORCA's 0.60 with far lower safety-human raises (0.30 vs 0.77). On the real robot after <4 h of training it beats the heuristic policy and sim-trained models: 146.3 steps to goal vs 158.0 for the heuristic, with 0.3 safety-human raises and 0.0 corridor raises.
limitations: Reward function is hand-tuned, and balancing path-tracking against human-avoidance terms is delicate.
Humans are modeled as circles, causing false positive and false negative collision detections.
Real-world tests use a limited set of behaviours from people familiar with the robot, not in-the-wild data; the CVMM check is overly conservative.
